Boomkat Product Review:
Glasgow's blush imprint build on the promise of last year's 'Shadow Garden' compilation with this gorgeous collection of slowcore, homespun folk and lo-fi avant whimsy, including exclusive tracks from soccer Committee and featuring more eaze, Natalia Panzer and a member of Princ€ss alongside a host of enigmatic outsiders who are mostly new to us. If you’ve melted into pretty much anything compiled by DJ Sundae or Time is Away, are a Grouper obsessive, or obsessed with that recent album from Cancer House - this is about as good as it gets.
Over just a handful of albums the blush label has established itself as an outpost for a kinda half-dreamed pop, hushed post-rock and fringe avant expression that labels like Les Disques Du Crépuscule and 4AD made their names on. The label’s first comp 'Shadow Garden' offered a patchwork of bedroom whimsy and crackling ambiance that linked languid dreamers like The Humble Bee, Shiner and TIBSLC with ana reme's Natalia Panzer and the Durutti Column-inspired JS Donny. On the sequel, blush asserts its unique viewpoint even more clearly, leaning into psychedelic hypnagogia, introducing us to a litany of mysterious operatives wondering around with a hazed pacing.  
'you were so close' opens and closes with a pair of stunners from soccer Committee, the veteran Dutch singer-songwriter whose hushed, slow-mo reverberations have had us in a chokehold for the last couple of decades. From there, we head to Berlin for Perlah's 'Frail Bird', a track that appears to pick up where Cancer House's glorious debut 'The Moth' left off in Spring. Building on the foundations of day-zero post rock like Bark Psychosis, Perlah and vocalist pinnin moss draw out each sound, quietly deconstructing the music so each emotional part feels so much more intense, while California's Sta Dormida tinkers at the mid point between post-punk and dreampop by draping her Liz Fraser-esque vocals over shimmering guitar and a gothic bassline.
Naarm's Glen Rey. (aka Bluetung) interrupts his jazzy riffs and 'Spirit of Eden'-style keys with garbled, glitchy voices that sound as if they're being streamed through a duff wireless connection, and the mysterious Calendar Violet excavate a seam through early trip-hop and languid dream pop that never materialised at the time.
